title: Nobody Can Explain Why The Experience Feels Hard
excerpt: This situation describes interface difficulty that users can feel but cannot decompose into causes. The diagnostic evidence usually appears in hesitation, compensating behaviour, support demand, sales friction, and workarounds.
metaDescription: Explains why users report hard workflows without naming causes, and how observation and workaround analysis locate accumulated interface friction.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary: users can experience real difficulty without being able to name its causes

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

This situation occurs when users repeatedly report that an experience is hard, slow, confusing, or difficult to remember, but the team cannot identify what specifically is causing the difficulty. The feedback may come from support channels, NPS comments, sales calls, or stakeholder accounts. Teams may respond by restructuring navigation, simplifying the UI, or improving onboarding, yet the next cycle of feedback still describes the experience as hard.

The difficulty is real. It is not a communication problem or a perception problem. The diagnostic issue is that the difficulty is not located in one describable event. It emerges from the accumulated interaction of small frictions across a workflow. Each friction may be minor on its own, but the combined experience becomes difficult.

## Diffuse workflow difficulty is not decomposed by the person experiencing it

Users experience accumulated interface difficulty as a quality of the whole workflow, not as a sequence of named obstacles. A workflow may require too many interactions, contain marginally unclear individual steps, apply inconsistent visual hierarchy across screens, and use ambiguous state transitions. Users may still complete the workflow successfully, but the accumulated effect is experienced as hard.

When users are asked what was hard about a task, they often describe the experience rather than the cause. They may describe difficulty, confusion, slowness, or uncertainty about where to go. These descriptions are accurate as accounts of experience. They are not findings that identify which design decisions produced friction, where the friction compounded, or why the total workflow felt difficult.

Surveys and structured interviews can confirm that users experience difficulty. They do not reliably identify the causes of diffuse workflow difficulty, because the causes are distributed across patterns of interaction rather than concentrated in one memorable failure event.

## Self-report misses hesitation, repeated checking, and compensating behaviour

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats unexplained interface difficulty as an observational problem rather than a verbal-reporting problem. The relevant evidence is often visible in behaviour: hesitation, repeated checking, incorrect sequencing, duplicate actions, workarounds, and compensating patterns that users no longer notice as workarounds.

A user who works regularly with a difficult interface may develop learned sequences, mental shortcuts, or parallel tools that allow the work to continue despite friction. When asked how the task is performed, the user describes the compensating pattern. The user does not necessarily identify the interface failure that made the compensating pattern necessary.

This is why short, controlled usability tasks can miss the mechanism. Creative Navy's documentation describes the relevant evidence as most visible under real operational conditions, where time pressure, workflow dependencies, role boundaries, and routine compensations appear in context.

## Workarounds identify where the designed process is not trusted

Workarounds are diagnostic evidence when users build parallel processes alongside a designed interface. Examples include spreadsheets running beside a platform, email chains used as the coordination mechanism for a system intended to coordinate work, printed reference sheets beside a terminal, and handwritten checklists beside a software screen.

These parallel processes are not automatically evidence of poor training or poor change management. In this situation, they indicate that users have assessed the designed interface under working conditions and found part of it insufficient. The workaround is a silent indicator that the experience is hard in ways users have stopped trying to explain.

The location of the workaround is also evidence. A spreadsheet beside a case management system points to failure in the case management workflow. A printed checklist beside a configuration interface indicates that the configuration workflow does not communicate state reliably enough to be trusted without a paper backup. The workaround maps the failure even when users cannot name it.

## WCO/IPM: unexplained difficulty across an intergovernmental enforcement network

The World Customs Organization's IPM platform was already in production when Creative Navy was engaged. The platform served an intergovernmental enforcement community spanning most international trade. Officers and rights holders described the system as difficult to navigate, slow to operate during inspections, and hard to learn across administrations with different technical environments and institutional cultures.

The visible diagnostic evidence included parallel spreadsheets and email chains around the platform across multiple member administrations. The workarounds were not confined to one administration with a local technical constraint. Their spread indicated a design failure in the interface itself rather than only an implementation or connectivity issue.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed this through Sandbox Experiments, including interviews, workflow mapping, and remote observation with WCO teams and selected member administrations. Three user groups were characterised operationally: frontline inspection officers, intelligence analysts, and rights holder teams. Each group had different tasks, physical working conditions, and relationships to the same platform.

The observed causes were specific. Core inspection workflows required several screens and frequent section switching. Too many choices appeared per screen without a hierarchy that directed attention to what was actionable. The training burden was high because the information architecture reflected internal system structures rather than the workflows users needed to complete.

Post-redesign, WCO/IPM outcomes included a client-reported 78% reduction in officer training costs, a client-reported 67% increase in rights holder platform use, and a client-reported 20% increase in officer platform use. Workaround processes were reduced across member administrations, also client-reported. Usability validation involved 47 participants from Italy, Romania, Uzbekistan, Algeria, and Spain and was directly observed.

## Triopsis: difficulty visible in sales friction, support volume, and live workflow behaviour

Triopsis's workforce management SaaS platform had accumulated inconsistencies over years of development without a central UX framework. The difficulty appeared commercially before it appeared as a precise design diagnosis. New customers found the interface difficult to understand, support teams answered basic questions, and sales calls became interface explanation sessions rather than capability demonstrations.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method surfaced the causes through in-situ observation with schedulers working under real-time pressure conditions. The observed conditions included weather incidents, conflicting locations, overlapping jobs, and crew shortages. Three sessions showed hesitation points, repeated checking, and error patterns including incorrect sequencing and duplicate assignments.

The 47-microtask analysis decomposed what in-situ observation had revealed into specific workflow and interaction failures. In the live system, product analytics recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning. Commercial outcomes were CEO-reported: sales conversions increased fourfold, and the client began winning clients four to five times larger.

## Egma: a heatmap located hesitation that stakeholder accounts could not explain

Egma is a Dubai-based ophthalmic lens manufacturer whose B2B lens ordering platform, Egma Order, was rebuilt by Creative Navy. Egma's marketing manager described the effect of the interface difficulty: customers did not appear to discover premium options, the platform lacked an immediately obvious sense of branding, and buttons and content appeared to be placed without a clear user journey.

The difficulty was located through a heatmap produced during the engagement. The heatmap identified three regions of the order form where users hesitated: the end of the left-hand column, the two primary actions at the bottom right, and the right-hand technology area, which users passed over.

The Egma heatmap is reported as an observation, not as a measurement. The instrument and capture method are not on record. No participant number, duration, rate, failure count, or baseline is attached to the heatmap, and it is not used as post-launch evidence. It is not eye-tracking.

## Handheld command-and-control review: scoring converted hard experience into ranked action

For a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them, Creative Navy led and co-authored an eighteen-page expert review of the running product with the client's design team.

The review contained two long-form argument sections, a four-part heuristic evaluation, a flow and information-architecture assessment, a visual-design assessment, an accessibility assessment, and a challenges-and-opportunities section. Every heuristic used a two-axis scoring scheme: current state on a three-point scale and effort to fix on a three-point scale.

The scoring scheme pre-sorted findings by what was worst and what was cheapest to address. In this engagement, the explanation did not come from field observation. It came from structured expert review, hands-on use of the running product, the client's brief, the client's observations, and published literature. Creative Navy has no primary field evidence for this engagement. The interface was built, with no further status claim made here.

## Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses the diagnostic gap

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses this situation by not relying on users to explain diffuse difficulty. Explanation requires decomposition, and users experiencing accumulated friction often cannot decompose the experience into causes.

The Sandbox Experiments phase is used to locate what self-report cannot: hesitation points, compensating behaviours, workaround patterns, and the operational conditions under which friction accumulates. Domain learning is necessary because the researcher must distinguish between genuine domain complexity and interface friction. In the WCO/IPM engagement, observation of inspection workflows required enough understanding of customs intelligence processes to make that distinction.

The output is an operational account of where the design is failing and why. This turns a broad description, such as difficult navigation, into specific workflow failures, decision points, and interaction failures that can be prioritised and addressed through design decisions.

## Boundaries and evidence limits

The examples on this page do not establish that all interface difficulty has the same cause. They describe a recurring situation where difficulty is real but distributed across workflow friction, compensating behaviour, and workarounds.

The WCO/IPM adoption and training outcomes are client-reported. The WCO/IPM usability validation involved 47 participants and was directly observed. The Triopsis performance outcomes are measured from product analytics of the live system, while Triopsis commercial outcomes are CEO-reported. The Egma heatmap is an observation only, with no recorded participant count, duration, rate, failure count, or baseline. The handheld command-and-control engagement was an expert review, not fieldwork.

No engagement dates are stated on this page. Sequence and duration are used only where available from the documented engagements.

## Related pages

This situation is related to software that is too complex for users, research that is not informing decisions, high training burden, unclear system state, and products that work in demonstrations but not in real use. The Triopsis, Egma, and tactical handheld command-and-control case studies provide grounded examples of how diffuse difficulty appears in different forms of evidence.
